challenges.name: picking-the-right-double-quiz
challenges.title: Pick the double, spot the over-specification
challenges.description: Four scenarios from the shop's test suites and one test of placeOrder. Decide which double fits each job, and which assertion will break on a harmless refactor.

questions.question: Which of these pairings of scenario and test double are good choices? (Select all that apply.)
questions.explanation: A dummy is right when a collaborator is required by the constructor but never used on the path under test: the coupon path never touches the logger, so {} is enough (and a crash would tell you the assumption is wrong). A stub is right when the code needs an answer from a collaborator: the tax rate is an input, and the test checks the resulting total (state verification). The stub mailer is wrong: it always resolves, so it cannot tell whether an email was sent, how many, or to whom, and it can never fail - which is exactly how the password-reset outage went unnoticed. Use a spy or a fake mailer with an outbox, and a double that rejects to test the outage path. Replacing a method of the payment provider's SDK in every checkout test is wrong: you do not own that interface, your double encodes your guess of how it behaves, and every checkout test is coupled to the SDK's shape. Wrap the SDK in a small payments adapter you own, fake the adapter in checkout tests, and test the adapter itself in a few tests against the provider's sandbox.

options.text: Testing that a coupon gives 10% off. The cart service requires a logger, but the coupon path never calls it: pass a dummy {}.
Testing the order total for a German customer: stub the tax service so taxRate("DE") resolves to 19, then assert the total in cents.
Testing that a password-reset email is sent exactly once: a stub mailer whose send() always resolves, then assert requestReset returned { status: "email sent" }.
Testing checkout payments: in every checkout test, replace the provider SDK's client.charges.create with t.mock.method and assert the exact SDK request object.

questions.explanation: D is over-specified: how many times placeOrder reads its own price cache is an implementation detail no customer can observe, so a harmless refactor (one batched lookup instead of two single ones) turns it red. A checks state - the outcome the customer pays - and survives any refactor that keeps the price right. B checks the outbox of a fake mailer: the confirmation email is a real outcome, and checking the template list (not the internal call sequence) leaves the service free to build the email however it likes. C is interaction verification, but here the interaction IS the outcome: charging the card exactly once with the right amount is the business rule, so counting the calls to the payments adapter is correct.

options.text: D - the number of price-cache reads is an internal detail; the batched lookup changes it while the order stays the same.
A - asserting the exact total couples the test to the pricing code.
B - tests should never look at emails, only at return values.
C - verifying calls to any double is always over-specification; the charge should not be checked.

challenges.name: build-a-spy
challenges.title: Build your own spy
challenges.description: Implement createSpy(impl), a small subset of node:test's t.mock.fn: it records every call (arguments, result, error, this), re-throws errors, counts calls, queues one-off implementations with mockImplementationOnce and forgets its history with resetCalls. The grader checks the spy directly, then uses it as the mailer double in a password-reset test suite - which must pass for the correct service and catch the services that swallow mailer errors or send the email twice.

tests.name: Records arguments, result and this for every call
A throwing implementation: the error is recorded, counted and the same error re-thrown
mockImplementationOnce queues implementations, used once each and in order
createSpy() returns undefined; resetCalls clears the history but keeps the queue
Your spy as the mailer double: the suite passes for the correct password-reset service
Your spy as the mailer double: the suite catches the service that swallows mailer errors
Your spy as the mailer double: the suite catches a bug you were not told about
